title: Skeleton of newly-discovered Nanotyrannus auctioned for $47.3m in New York
description: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has just been sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (£
body: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex has just been sold at auction for a colossal $47.3m (£35.5m).Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton was auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.The Late Cretaceous carnivore was expected to fetch at least $9m when it went under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m in July.The sale comes amid debate in the scientific community over whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately or displayed publicly.Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science". The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.The identify of the buyer, who won after a thrilling 12 minutes of auction bidding between six interested parties, has not been disclosed.Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex"."But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago."Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hell Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning"."I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."He said at the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.Responding to Tuesday's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view. "We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens."I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

schema.headline: Skeleton of newly-discovered Nanotyrannus auctioned for $47.3m in New York

title: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford
description: Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection to an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford in September.Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Wes
body: Two British nationals have appeared in court in connection to an alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford in September.Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, London, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, which police earlier said they believed to be Iran.  Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.The pair appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.The court heard vans bearing the logo "Fuel2You" were spotted close to the base. In the early hours, the vans came across a Ministry of Defence Police cordon and re-routed to another location.Police arrived and arrested five men. They later revealed that one had called 999 and reported what was going on.During the hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court, Essghir stood in the dock wearing a grey sweatshirt and confirmed his name and address.Abdulkarim is charged with helping with the plot.He appeared in court in a wheelchair wearing a checked shirt, jeans and a baseball cap. He confirmed his name and address.Both men are charged under the 2023 National Security Act.They were told the case will be next heard at the Old Bailey on 20 November.Essghir was one of five men arrested near the base on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them"."In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.US President Donald Trump at the time said he was "surprised" the men had been released, saying: "We would not have released them."Taylor said counter-terror police had seen "a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state".Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America. Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

schema.headline: Two in court over alleged Iran-linked plot at RAF Fairford

title: Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah detained after court orders Mada Masr's closure
description: The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr has been taken into custody after a court convicted her of managing an unlicense
body: The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr has been taken into custody after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers say.Lina Attalah will be held until she pays the fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100) also handed down by the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court. It was the maximum possible penalty for the charge, which she had rejected.The human rights group Amnesty International said the verdict represented "a crushing blow to press freedom".It comes only weeks after six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ).President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013.Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics.The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism.The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added.Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting.Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence.Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status.Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence.During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group.Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah."In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes."In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added.The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat.Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned."This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed."Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job."CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."

schema.headline: Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah detained after court orders Mada Masr's closure

title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
description: British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told th
body: British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us. "We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit."He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be."But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement."We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election."I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

schema.headline: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement

title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
description: Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese
body: Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands. Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football. "My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world,"  Mbappé said in a statement."I apologise to everyone my words have upset."Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.  The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator". Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".  Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.  Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public"."International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another  comment on Weibo.As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.  The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online. Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname. France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people"."There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said."Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."Additional reporting by Fan Wang and Osmond Chia

schema.headline: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China

title: Wirral parents who killed their baby have sentences increased
description: A  couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-ye
body: A  couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, from Wirral, Merseyside, were sentenced in April to a minimum of 19 years and 15 years in April over the death of their son, 13-week-old Miguel.The Court of Appeal has now increased Klevi Pirjani's sentence to 21 years and six months, while Nivalda Pirjani will have to serve 17 years and nine months. Miguel was taken to Alder Hey children's hospital in November 2024. He had severe head injuries and died five days after being admitted.Miguel was found to have suffered 41 separate bone fractures in at least four separate incidents.The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves, referred their sentences to the Court of Appeal, with barristers for the government arguing that the original sentences did not "meet the justice of this terrible case".Lord Justice Jeremy Baker, sitting with Mr Justice Goose and Mr Justice Hilliard, said the pair subjected their son to "routine" assaults which increased in severity, and culminated in his "particularly callous" murder.He said: "We take the view that the resulting sentences significantly underestimated the aggravating factors, to the extent that not only do we consider that the minimum terms were unduly lenient, but that we should set them aside."Bill Emlyn Jones KC, for the Attorney General, said in written submissions that Miguel's death was caused by an assault by his parents on 24 November 2024, which involved "a heavy blow, or series of blows, to the right side of his head".Paramedics arrived two minutes after his parents called 999 following Miguel suffering a cardiac arrest at their home in Percy Road, Seacombe, Merseyside, but he never regained consciousness and was pronounced dead five days later.Emlyn Jones said that while the boy was in hospital, a "wider picture of long-standing physical abuse emerged", including the discovery of multiple fractured ribs, fractured legs and a fractured sternum suffered across several incidents before the fatal attack.He also said that while it could not be ascertained whether Klevi Pirjani or Nivalda Pirjani inflicted the fatal violence, "whichever it was, they did so with the encouragement of their partner".Sentencing them in March, Mr Justice Andrew Baker said the pair were "in this together, encouraging each other" to attack their "defenceless" son.He said that who "fatally battered" the infant "remains the guilty secret of a warped relationship, in which you came first for each other to an unnatural degree".Rupert Bowers KC, for Nivalda Pirjani, acknowledged in court that "of course" her sentence was lenient, but that the sentencing judge "considered all of the factors".He said: "There is nothing that would indicate that the sentences he passed are beyond the ambit of reasonableness, or an error of principle, so that this court should interfere with his exercise of discretion, having heard all the evidence."Sarah Vine KC, for Klevi Pirjani, also said her client's sentence was "undoubtedly lenient, but not unduly, and leniency in itself is not a vice".Klevi and Nivalda Pirjani, watching proceedings from HMP Wakefield in Yorkshire and HMP Styal in Cheshire respectively, showed no reaction as their sentences were increased.

schema.headline: Wirral parents who killed their baby have sentences increased

title: Was the Ballon d'Or in London the most chaotic?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Ballon d'Or ceremony began at 20:45 GMT instead of 20:00 because of traffic issuesBySarah DawkinsBBC Spor
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Ballon d'Or ceremony began at 20:45 GMT instead of 20:00 because of traffic issuesBySarah DawkinsBBC Sport senior journalistIt was the first time the Ballon d'Or had been held in London in its 70-year history, with organisers choosing the iconic London Palladium as the venue.Despite the perfect homecoming for Harry Kane on Monday night, the rest of the event was not plain sailing.Did the organisers give away the winners early or was it just a simple mix-up? Why was the ceremony delayed and why was the audience booing?BBC Sport assesses a chaotic night in central London.Traffic, delay and a rowdy audienceLondon traffic can cause issues on any day but unfortunately for the Ballon d'Or organisers, they chose to hold a major event just a stone's throw from Oxford Street on the same day the famous shopping area was made traffic-free.That, coupled with large crowds at the event entrance, meant significant numbers of guests were delayed and the start had to be pushed back by 45 minutes.Once it did get under way, a rowdy and boisterous audience sat through a ceremony that lasted nearly two and a half hours. On a number of occasions, hosts Kate Scott and Thierry Henry had to briefly pause proceedings while people shouted the names of players in the audience and there were several instances of booing during commercial breaks.After Kane and Alexia Putellas had been crowned the winners in the two main categories, they then spoke to the world's media in separate press conferences.Journalists were able to put questions to Putellas but only men were selected to ask Kane a question, with several female journalists having their attempts seemingly ignored.The Ballon d'Or team has since apologised.Clashes with policeHundreds of people gathered outside the London Palladium to try to get a glimpse of the biggest stars in football on the red carpet. A security perimeter of metal fencing and barricades had been erected to try to keep those without a ticket out.But the BBC Sport team witnessed those barriers being scaled, broken and ripped down and several people being evicted by security after making their way through.The atmosphere at times was tense, with footage on social media appearing to show fans clashing with security and police.The BBC has approached the Metropolitan Police for comment.Website blunderThe confusion and chaos began hours before the ceremony had even started, after the official Ballon d'Or website published an article declaring Kane as the winner of the men's award.Further digging revealed similar articles had been published about some of the other favourites to win the men's and women's awards, including Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe and London City Lionesses' Putellas.Was it a genuine mistake? Or a case of trying to divert people's attention from the initial Kane announcement? Which of course turned out to be true.A Ballon d'Or spokesperson told BBC Sport last night they were "inadvertently published online"."These articles had been prepared for all nominees and should in no way be considered as an indication of the final results or rankings," the spokesperson said.The Ballon d'Or official social media accounts also mixed up the names of two of the women's nominees, congratulating 'Alexia Bonmati' on her victory. The post was later deleted.

schema.headline: Was the Ballon d'Or in London the most chaotic?

title: Venus Williams: Former world number one loses to Lilli Tagger at Guangzhou Open
description: Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles - plus 30 WTA tournaments - before Austria's Tagger was born in February 2008.Tagger's coach Frances
body: Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles - plus 30 WTA tournaments - before Austria's Tagger was born in February 2008.Tagger's coach Francesca Schiavone - the Italian former world number four who won the 2010 French Open - is the same age as Williams, and lost all eight meetings with the American during her playing career."When I saw the draw I was super excited and a bit nervous - I respect her a lot," said Tagger, who is 53rd in the world."It is funny she used to play with my coach. I would love to play at this age - I want to congratulate her."While the straight-set scoreline will embolden the critics, Williams did make Tagger - a rising talent who is predicted to have a bright future at the very top - work hard.However, the teenager proved far too good. The 2025 French Open girls' champion was superb on serve - dropping just seven service points and not facing a break point - while handling Williams' pace and crushing groundstrokes off both wings.Tagger broke her illustrious opponent's serve twice - for 1-0 and 5-2 leads - in two almost identical sets.At times, Williams was able to use her powerful serve to get out of trouble - fighting off 12 of 16 break points - and the veteran's trademark competitive spirit never wavered.But it was another example of how far behind the rest of the tour she now is.

schema.headline: Venus Williams: Former world number one loses to Lilli Tagger at Guangzhou Open

title: Michael Carrick to stay in charge of Man Utd for Chelsea game
description: Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their trip to Chelsea this weekend.Sources have told BBC Sport that the 45-year-old wil
body: Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their trip to Chelsea this weekend.Sources have told BBC Sport that the 45-year-old will be given the opportunity to turn things around at Old Trafford following a dismal start to the campaign. Carrick oversaw training on Tuesday morning, as United look to end a run of eight matches without a win in all competitions when they visit Stamford Bridge on Saturday. Sunday's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford plunged Carrick's future into doubt, with United sitting one place above the relegation zone.It is understood United's hierarchy have explored the possibility of replacing Carrick, with ex-Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann under consideration.But sources have told BBC Sport that the former Middlesbrough manager will not only take charge against Chelsea but will also be given a chance to revive the club's fortunes on the pitch. Carrick took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim's departure and he was rewarded with the permanent job in May after securing Champions League qualification with an impressive run that resulted in them finishing third.But United's form has collapsed this term, with Carrick's side winning just one of their eight Premier League matches so far this season.Defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's board for a lack of investment following United's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League earlier this month.Captain Bruno Fernandes then took aim at Carrick's tactics following a humiliating 4-1 loss against Como in their next Champions League fixture.The Portuguese was dropped to the bench for Sunday's loss to Bournemouth, and remained an unused substitute.United supporters chanted Carrick's name as the former England international made his way to the tunnel after the match, but quickly directed boos at the players once Carrick had made his way off the pitch.Carrick gestured towards the Stretford End as they chanted his name after the match."It wasn't a farewell from me," Carrick said on Sky Sports."I've mixed emotions, I'm feeling it for my players, they're going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment."Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way. To have that connection with the supporters it's mixed emotions, it'll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support."The situation is where we are and we haven't had results or performances that have been good enough."Carrick was at also United's training ground on Monday morning, despite the first team being given the day off. Director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada were both pictured arriving at the club's training ground on Monday, with Carrick leaving at about 17:00 GMT. Howe, 48, is available after leaving Newcastle United last summer but any club that hires the Englishman will have to pay a multi-million pound compensation package to the Magpies after he resigned from his post with three years remaining on his deal. Nagelsmann, 39, resigned as Germany boss following their quarter-final exit at the 2026 World Cup and is aware of United's interest in him. Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.Manchester United might be trying to pass this off as business as usual but the reality is anything but. The mere fact there was no clarification around Carrick's future on Monday - both before and after he was at the training ground to watch an Under-21 game his son Jacey was part of, or on Tuesday after his 07:30 arrival at Carrington and the 11:00 training start time, fuels theories and speculation, which just adds to the air of uncertainty. Carrick will be in charge at Stamford Bridge, but what about Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday and Aston Villa after that? Given the woeful nature of their last two performances, how will United's players respond at Chelsea when the spotlight on them is so fierce? Can Carrick drag a performance out of them? Has he made his peace with skipper Bruno Fernandes? Is director of football Jason Wilcox safe? There are still so many unanswered questions. Last season's win at Stamford Bridge was one of the key results in securing Carrick the head coach's job permanently. Will the next trip there be the start of a brighter future or mark the end of his tenure?

schema.headline: Michael Carrick to stay in charge of Man Utd for Chelsea game

title: Oleshky ceasefire begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByDan JohnsonReporting fromKyiv and Olga MalchevskaUpdated 1 hour agoA truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian cit
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByDan JohnsonReporting fromKyiv and Olga MalchevskaUpdated 1 hour agoA truce has begun in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents have been trapped without food, water and electricity.Ukrainian officials and Russia's defence ministry say the limited ceasefire is being respected. The truce, which the White House said was secured by US First Lady Melania Trump, is meant to allow aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation on Friday. Oleshky, along the front line in the Kherson region, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and on the other by Russian forces.Many residents have resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive, telling the BBC they are suffering extreme hunger and want to leave.There are concerns that the truce will not hold, with one resident saying: "I don't believe in Russia's humanity."Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, remain in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, Kyiv believes, with only 1,700 still living in the city itself.Before the war it was home to 24,000 people, but it was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.  Conditions have become so desperate that not only is getting supplies into the city extremely difficult, but escape is highly dangerous because the routes out of Oleshky have been mined and subject to drone attack.No shops are open, and the city has had no electricity, gas or water for three years.Pope Leo XIV appealed earlier this month to Russia's President Vladimir Putin to allow food and medical aid into Oleshky as well as a safe evacuation, and urged his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to co-operate with Moscow over a ceasefire.The current truce is supposed to allow supplies in and enable roads to be cleared of mines to allow people safe passage out in an evacuation planned to take place on Friday.One woman told the BBC she had stepped on a land mine and was currently in hospital where she had undergone two operations."I don't know how long I will have to spend there," she said, worried about not being able to join the evacuation.Many told the BBC last month there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.It is hard to make contact with people in Oleshky as communication is patchy and many are reluctant to speak of the situation in fear of reprisals from the Russians, making it difficult to verify reports the ceasefire is being implemented.Many details on the evacuation plans are unclear, initially including how and where to register for it. Some people want to know if they can bring their pets. Others are questioning what future they will have if they opt to leave their homes."It is critically important that this mission to rescue our people proceeds successfully and safely," Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Zelensky's office, said on Tuesday.Russia's defence ministry said units from the army's Dnepr group had been conducting "engineering reconnaissance" and clearing main access roads into the village of "explosive and booby-trap devices". While people are optimistic about leaving, there are also fears that Russia may not allow them to return to Ukraine, or examine their phones and online activity for signs of Ukrainian support, which could see them be taken away and tortured. Someone who has been speaking to family in Oleshky said they fear shooting could restart during evacuations and Ukraine will somehow be blamed for not upholding the truce.Image source, Ksenia ArkhipovaImage caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this yearLast month, the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.In response to the situation, the White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured a ceasefire.Russia's defence ministry said on Telegram it had stopped firing toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson - across the river from Oleshky - at 04:00 Moscow time (03:00 in Ukraine; 01:00 GMT) in preparation for the humanitarian operation.The truce is due to be in place until 23:59 local time on 1 November, according to Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament.Ukrainian officials say parliament's commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, has travelled to the areas to co-ordinate the operation."This is part of a humanitarian mission being carried out with the mediation and co-ordination of US First Lady Melania Trump, in co-operation with Yana Lantratova, Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights," Lubinets wrote on social media.Ukraine's military general staff said that silence was being observed over the operation for humanitarian purposes, and urged people not to trust unverified reports or spread rumours about "the routes, time and place of the movement of people and humanitarian convoys".Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro LubinetsImage caption, Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trappedZelensky has warned that routes out of Oleshky that are demined by Russia will ensure that those civilians leaving Oleshky will "head towards Russia and stay there". However, he said some would get to Ukrainian-controlled territory "one way or another", and ideally anyone trapped would be able to reach their destination and evacuate to Ukraine.One resident called Serhii, who fled Oleshky around three weeks ago, has told the BBC how he walked 24km (15 miles) of minefields to get to safety."In some places you have to keep two metres away. In others you have to walk quietly... you can't even talk. We passed within a metre of mines like that, hoping they wouldn't go off," he said.Serhii, who did not want to share his surname, said he had eventually returned to Ukraine via Russia and Belarus but called for a route across the River Dnipro that avoided Russian-occupied territory, saying "you simply cannot trust the Russian Federation".However, bridges across the river have been destroyed and sources say the riverbank is also mined and dangerous.The White House said last week that "non-military, civilian leaders from both countries would work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require".Although the US first lady is relatively lower-profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".While a truce is under way in Oleshky, elsewhere strikes continue. On Monday evening, attacks on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv hit a university and a bridge, killing one person and injuring 14 others.In Russia, one person was killed and six others were injured after a Ukrainian drone strike on Bryansk.Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko, Paul Kirby, Hafsa Khalil and Sareen Habeshian

schema.headline: Oleshky ceasefire begins in Ukraine city where residents ate weeds to survive

title: Formula 1 next engine regulations to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines
description: Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existi
body: Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existing rules.A proposal document sent by governing body the FIA to the six manufacturers in F1 outlines a framework for discussions on engines to be introduced in either 2030 or 2031.Multiple sources within F1 have provided BBC Sport with the details within the document.The plan, which comes after initial discussions with individual engine manufacturers on a one-to-one basis, proposes cheaper, lighter, simpler engines with a more visceral sound.However, the FIA has moved away from its initial proposal to return to naturally aspirated engines.The stated aim of the new rules is to introduce lighter, more responsive cars, increased emphasis on driver skill, relevant technologies, reduced cost, to make it easier for new manufacturers to enter F1 and to continue with the sport's commitment to reducing emissions.This comes after criticism of the new engines introduced this year for their complexity and the way their design and operation has diminished the driving challenge of some of F1's best corners.The proposal changes the previous stance of the FIA on naturally aspirated engines - president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially proposed a return of V10s at the start of last year and has more recently been pushing V8s.The addition of the turbo satisfies the need for the engines to be road-relevant, as well as increasing efficiency and requiring less fuel than a pure naturally aspirated engine.The published proposals can be seen as a kind of middle ground between Ben Sulayem's initial stance, the desire of at least some manufacturers to keep turbos and a significant hybrid element, and a recognition that the latest rules were flawed in concept and execution.The new engines will have none of the problems of energy starvation about which drivers have complained this season.Fernando Alonso has called F1 the "battery world championship" and described fast corners as "the charging station for the car", while Max Verstappen has described the new rules  as "Formula E on steroids" and anti-racing.Both have since tempered their criticisms having seen that the sport's bosses have listened to their comments on the engines and made immediate changes to the rules this year as well as started working towards a new direction in the future.The fundamental framework of the proposal for the new engine's architecture is said to be basically acceptable to all the manufacturers.However, the details around how the rules operate will need discussion.The document outlines two possible ways forward for the new rule set.One is aimed at minimising necessary adaptation - for example, a 2.1-litre V8 could be produced by simply adding two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre blocks and reducing the size of the turbo and MGU-K (hybrid motor).The other, more controversial, is to have an external manufacturer design and supply a baseline power-unit with a high degree of standardisation, on to which manufacturers could add a degree of customisation.However, insiders say the manufacturers are all aligned on wanting to design and build their own power-units and for engines to remain a performance differentiator.The companies who currently supply engines to F1 teams are Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi, Honda and Red Bull. Cadillac, which entered F1 this year with its own team, is planning to produce an engine to the new rules.There are two further arguments to steer away from the standardisation route:The first is that the reasons for it - to safeguard against manufacturers leaving the sport - is irrelevant as all six will be committed under the new rule set.The second is that the standardisation of electronics control units this season has led to a series of problems, such as at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when cars were restricted to not much more than walking pace because of a software bug.The document outlines a proposal to cut the engine budget cap by 50% from the current level of $190m (£143m) per year.However, this is considered a starting point for discussions, while there are also concerns about providing a suitable glide path down to the new number to enable teams to manage the impact on workforces.Discussions around the budget cap also involve the need to balance ongoing development of the existing engines with design and construction of the new ones.That topic is interlinked with whether the new rules will come into force in 2030 or 2031.The existing contracts in F1 bind the FIA, teams and commercial rights holder together only until 2030.Ben Sulayem has previously threatened to introduce his own rules unilaterally in 2031.That threat appears to have receded and the process has been marked by a spirit of co-operation, which is expected to continue.An FIA spokesperson declined to comment on or discuss the document, pointing instead to an Instagram post published on Ben Sulayem's account outlining the aims and objectives of of the new rules., external It makes no mention of turbos or hybrid technology.The aim is for discussions over the next weeks to lead to a proposal that can be put to F1's legislative body, the FIA world council, in December.

schema.headline: Formula 1 next engine regulations to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines

title: US midterm elections: Trump's biggest economic problem looks familiar
description: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiarImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US President Donald Trump and his predecessor
body: Donald Trump's biggest economic problem looks strangely familiarImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US President Donald Trump and his predecessor Joe BidenByMichelle FleuryNew York business correspondentThe White House is confronting a familiar dilemma. The economic numbers aren't necessarily bad - but the public mood is.It's a disconnect that haunted Joe Biden in 2024, when solid headline data failed to convince many voters that the economy was working for them.Now, Donald Trump faces a version of the same challenge.During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised voters swift relief from rising prices."When I win, I will immediately bring prices down," he said.Delivering on that promise has proved harder than expected. Economic growth is holding up, unemployment remains low and the stock market is near record highs.Yet the final inflation report ahead of the midterm elections confirms what voters already know: prices remain high.The causes are different. Biden was grappling with the aftermath of the Covid pandemic. Trump faces higher energy prices linked to the US-Israel conflict with Iran and the fallout from some of his own trade and immigration policies.The political reality, however, is much the same. Voters are not judging the economy by GDP figures or record highs on the stock market. They are judging it by what they pay at the supermarket, petrol prices and whether they can keep up with the bills.Numbers only tell part of the storyUS economic growth of 2.2% would be respectable by the standards of many wealthy economies. Germany, for example, has struggled to generate comparable momentum. And a stable US unemployment rate of 4.2% hardly suggests an economy in freefall.Trump argues that he inherited an economic mess from Biden, and points to strong growth, investment and stock market performance as evidence that his policies are working.Following the most recent inflation report, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said the administration's "aggressive, pro-growth economic agenda" had blunted "Biden's inflation crisis".Larry Kudlow, a Trump ally and economic commentator, has described the current expansion as "the greatest story never told", external, arguing that "nobody is getting fired".But voters appear to be reading a different story - one in which Trump won the presidency promising to tackle the cost of living, only for prices to keep rising.Part of the problem is that wage increases have not kept pace with prices. Average hourly earnings have risen 3% over the last year, while consumer prices have increased 3.7%.That helps explain why polls continue to show voters giving Trump poor marks for his handling of the economy.Same language, different meaningsFor Democrats, the dynamic feels familiar.Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, says the problem begins with the way economists and voters use the same language to mean different things."When economists say inflation comes down, they mean the rate of increase has come down," she says."When voters say inflation has come down, they mean the price has returned to what it was. Well, of course, it never returns to what it was."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Joe Biden campaigned in 2024 on the economy but voters saw things differently  The Biden administration spent much of 2024 highlighting low unemployment, solid growth and falling inflation. However, many voters remained focused on the higher prices they faced every day.Lake, who advised Biden's 2020 campaign but was not involved in the 2024 race, says voters judge the economy through personal experience, not economic indicators."You can't argue with people about their own lived reality," she says.That may help explain why Trump's challenge looks so similar to Biden's.The Trump effectBiden's critics blamed him for inflation. But he could point to forces largely outside his control, including the pandemic and its supply chain aftershocks.Trump has less room to do that.Some economists argue that today's higher prices are at least partly the result of his own policies, including tariffs, as well as the economic fallout from the US-Israel war with Iran."The inflation is clearly traceable to Donald Trump," says Peter Morici, a University of Maryland economist who aligns with Republicans."It's his tariffs and the war. People know that. They see it."Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs, announced in April 2025, have added to costs for consumers.A study by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found the tariffs increased consumer goods prices by about 2.9%.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Donald Trump pledged to lower prices for US householdsThe impact might have been larger if Trump hadn't later paused some tariffs, struck new trade deals and been blocked by the Supreme Court from using emergency powers to impose many others.Then came another shock. Conflict with Iran pushed oil prices higher, lifting the cost of petrol and putting fresh pressure on household budgets.The White House points to tax cuts, job growth and lower prescription drug costs as evidence that the administration is delivering for American families. And it is increasingly embracing policies aimed at easing pressures.Trump has called for a cap on credit card interest rates and floated the idea of a $5,000 payment to American adults if Republicans retain control of Congress.The measures reflect a political reality familiar to both parties: when voters are anxious about prices, arguments about solid growth and low unemployment are rarely enough.Biden never found a way to bridge the gap between economic performance and economic sentiment. The question heading into the midterms is whether Trump can.If recent political history is any guide, perceptions of the economy may matter more than the economic data itself.

schema.headline: US midterm elections: Trump's biggest economic problem looks familiar

title: Men sexually assaulted Philip Young's wife after online ad, court told
description: Four men sexually assaulted a woman after her then-husband drugged her and advertised her on Craigslist, Grindr and swinging websites, a court has bee
body: Four men sexually assaulted a woman after her then-husband drugged her and advertised her on Craigslist, Grindr and swinging websites, a court has been told.Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, are on trial at Winchester Crown Court after pleading not guilty to sexual offences against Joanne Young.They are charged jointly with her ex-husband Philip Young, 50, a former councillor, who admitted to drugging and raping her over 13 years.As the trial began, prosecutor Sarah Jones KC told the jury: "This case is about whether it is ever reasonable to have sex with an unknown woman without checking with her first."Warning: This story contains distressing detailsJoanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, told police to her knowledge she had a "fairly normal" and "always monogamous" sex life with her husband. But on one occasion in 2023, she said she woke up with restraints and a blindfold on while a man who she thought was her husband, was carrying out a sexual act on her.Another man had his hand on her wrist, the court was told.Jones told the jury Joanne believed her husband was performing the sexual act on her when in reality he was "stage managing another unknown person" who was "taking his place without her knowledge".

schema.headline: Men sexually assaulted Philip Young's wife after online ad, court told

title: Thorpe St Andrew School attacker 'radicalised online', says dad
description: Boy who stabbed girl at school was radicalised online, says fatherImage source, ContributedImage caption, Armed police officers were called to Thorpe
body: Boy who stabbed girl at school was radicalised online, says fatherImage source, ContributedImage caption, Armed police officers were called to Thorpe St Andrew School after a teenage girl was stabbed by another pupilByRobby WestNorfolkWarning: The following report contains details that some may find distressingThe father of a teenager who tried to kill a fellow pupil in a school knife attack has described his devastation and belief that his son was "radicalised" by extreme material online.The boy, now 16, was found guilty of attempted murder last week after a trial heard how he harboured a hatred of women, had a fascination with serial killers and had planned to target others in the attack at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich.Speaking exclusively to the BBC and calling for tighter controls, the boy's father said he did not want to "absolve" his son but suggested online material and "a culture of violence and horror" had influenced him. The government said it was committed to ensuring all children were safe from radicalisation and threats online, pointing to its Prevent anti-terrorism scheme and the Online Safety Act, which compels social media platforms to remove and prevent the spread of illegal content.The boy cannot be identified due to his age, and nor can witnesses and the victim in the case.His father, who we are calling John, apologised to the 15-year-old girl injured in the attack on 11 March, saying: "We're so very sorry for what happened."John spoke of his fears that young men were being radicalised towards violence and hatred."You can think... it can never happen to my family or my son couldn't be involved, but that's what we thought and that wasn't the case," he said.Image source, Shaun Whitmore/BBCImage caption, John's son was convicted after a trial at King's Lynn Crown CourtA two-week trial at King's Lynn Crown Court heard how the boy dressed in black and wore a face mask to stab the girl with a kitchen knife.John described his own "rising feeling of panic" on the day of the attack.He said he and his wife had been "fearful for what he might have done and fearful for what would happen to him".But John said he only learned the full details when they emerged during the trial. "It was awful, really devastating," he said.He acknowledged the attack would have had "major repercussions" for the victim, who spent a night in hospital but was not seriously injured."I hope the victim and her family can sort of get over it as soon as possible in terms of healing and move on," he said.Image source, Qays Najm/BBCImage caption, Roads around the school were cordoned off following the attackBefore the attack, John said, his family had been "normal".His son was shy but had a group of friends and had been "kind and thoughtful" at home.As a teenager, he began to spend more time on his own, but John saw nothing concerning.However, police later found the boy had searched the internet for material on mass shootings and serial killers, including on the night before the attack - something John said he had "no idea" about."It was shocking and devastating that he would have been looking at that kind of stuff," he said.While there were parental controls on his son's devices, these were mainly to limit screen time."There was nothing to indicate that anything sinister was going on," said John.If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, you can visit the BBC Action Line for information and supportAsked if they should have known more about what was on their son's phone, he said: "I can see the argument."I doubt many parents will go through their kids' browsing history on a regular basis."Hindsight's a marvellous thing, isn't it?"Image source, Crown Prosecution ServiceImage caption, The kitchen knife used to stab the victim had a blade measuring 18cm (7in) and a handle measuring 12cm (5in) and was found in a wooded areaWhen police searched the family home after the attack, they found the boy had written notes planning a wider attack.They talked about deaths and injuries, listing misanthropy, misogyny, suicide, bullying as motives.John said reading the notes made him feel "physically sick"."It's still perplexing to us that he would write those things and feel those things that he was feeling," he said."He just seems like a different person doing that; some different version of him that's emerged from whatever he's been watching or seeing online."John said his son had told him he believed his interest in extreme violence began after he saw a clip on TikTok from TV drama Dexter, which tells the story of a vigilante serial killer."Once you watch one thing like that, the algorithm, of course, feeds you more of the same content," he said.He said he believed some young men could be drawn towards increasingly extreme material online and called for tighter regulations on children's access to it."There's the radicalisation of young men in particular. They talk about it with regards to terrorism and political ideology, but [there's] a radicalisation towards violence and hatred," he said."There must be ways to block content or to monitor content. We see millions of pounds spent on other things. Is there enough being spent on this kind of thing?"What can parents do?Ofcom, the official regulator for broadcasting and the internet, says it is the responsibility of tech firms to keep children safe online.It says it is holding those companies to account, but has the following tips for parents, external:Talk regularly to your children about what they do when they're online.Make sure your children register with online services using their real age, to help prevent them from accessing content that is only suitable for people who are older.Make sure they know how to report inappropriate or harmful content, how to block accounts that share it and encourage them not to share it themselves. If content is illegal, report it to the police.Parental controls are a useful tool, helping you to monitor and limit the time your children spend online, and what they do when they're there.Image source, NetflixImage caption, John acknowledged parallels with his son's crime and the storyline of award-winning drama Adolescence starring Owen Cooper (left) and Stephen GrahamThe attack by John's son had parallels with the storyline of hit Netflix drama Adolescence, which shows the aftermath of the fatal stabbing of a teenage girl by a fellow school pupil.It highlighted the corrosive impact of social media and misogynist influencers on some teenage boys and prompted then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer to pledge to tackle the issue.John said while he had not personally watched the show, he was aware of discussion around it and could see why links to it might be made."Knowing what it was about did prompt a chat with our son about the manosphere and those sort of toxic influencers it references," he said.Notes written by John's son expressed a hatred of women, and he had also researched Elliot Rodger, described to jurors as "an early influence on incel and manosphere culture".But John said his son had never shown evidence of misogyny."He's always got on well with all the women he's known in his life... there's never been a problem."Image source, ContributedImage caption, Pictures shared with the BBC showed some children hiding underneath their desks after the school was put under lockdownJohn said the family believed their son was dealing with mental health issues in the months before the attack.He had wanted to self-harm and had attempted to take his own life, he said. "We were worried about what he might do to himself."John urged other parents not to be afraid to be "a bit intrusive" into their children's lives, adding: "Try and have a proper chat. It's difficult to find the time sometimes because you're wrapped up in your own things."In a statement, a government spokesman said its thoughts were with the victim and all of those affected by the "terrible events" at Thorpe St Andrew School."We are committed to ensuring all children are safe from radicalisation and threats online," they said."Prevent plays a crucial role in this, moving more than 6,000 people away from violent ideologies since 2015."In addition, social media platforms must be able to remove illegal content and stop children accessing harmful material by law – or face penalties of up to £18m for failing to comply."John acknowledged that his son was "looking at a long sentence" when he appears before the court again in December."We will support him as best we can, try and see that he gets the mental health support he needs and try and get back how he used to be," he said.Follow Norfolk news on BBC Sounds, Facebook, external, Instagram, external and X, external.

schema.headline: Thorpe St Andrew School attacker 'radicalised online', says dad

title: What do you want from the Budget? 'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40'
description: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma Crew
body: Image caption, Chloe, Emily and Robert all spoke to the BBC about what they would like to see in the BudgetByDaniel ThomasKris Bramwell and Jemma CrewUpdated 3 hours agoChancellor John Healey is set to unveil his first Budget on Wednesday.Unlike in previous years there have been very few leaks about what will be in it, though Healey's tax and spending plans will be under close scrutiny at a time when government borrowing costs are at "historic highs".BBC News has been speaking to people on a range of incomes on how they feel about their finances and what they would like to see in the Budget.If there are issues you would like to see covered, you can get in touch via BBC Your Voice.Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living. She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about £200 a month on gas and electricity."We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to £40.But she can't do anything to reduce her £200 council tax bill, the £250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as £50.Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families."I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."'I earn £22,000. Saving for a house is impossible'Robert Portlock, 29, has always lived with his parents in Gateshead and would love to move out. But he doesn't think he can afford to.Rent would be his biggest concern, he says, explaining that a small flat in his area would cost him about two-thirds of his monthly wage.   "Council tax and energy bills would add to it. Food too. I'd need a TV licence, broadband, my car and some money to socialise. By that point I'd be in the minus."Robert's biggest expense currently is his car, which he says he needs for his 32-mile round trip to work at Newcastle Airport. But he's paying £750 a month in car finance, insurance, fuel and tax. He wants the chancellor to cut fuel duty and income tax, or increase the personal allowance - the amount of income you do not have to pay tax on - to about £16,000, up from £12,570 currently. He would like to get on the housing ladder but for now it feels a distant prospect. The government has announced a scheme to help first-time buyers in England who have a deposit of 2.5%, but Robert says: "Saving for a house is impossible at the moment."'I get £4,062 in universal credit. I'm trying my best'Emily Nelson completed her A-levels last year and like thousands of her peers has been unable to find a job since leaving college. The 19-year-old from Swindon wants to be an animator but in the meantime is applying for retail and sales roles and apprenticeships. Most of the time, she doesn't hear back from potential employers."I'm trying my best, it's all you really can do. It's kind of suffocating in a way. You see everyone else managing, and you feel like you're not."She wants the government to provide more funding to businesses so they can take on more young employees. She'd also like to see more money for training and the government's Jobs Guarantee, external scheme extended.The scheme, being rolled out across England, Scotland and Wales, guarantees fully funded, six-month paid jobs for 18 to 24-year-olds who have been on universal credit and looking for work for 18 months. But Emily thinks people should be eligible after a year.She is living with her parents but wants to move out eventually. "My parents want me to get a job first. They are not putting pressure on me to go yet."'I earn £30,000 and dread filling up my car'Dave Herbert, a professional driver who moves cars between showrooms and does deliveries, says fuel prices have been "crazy" this year.He spends around £350 a month on petrol for work and personal use. That's 40% to 50% more than at the start of the year, he says.He has to commute into Cardiff, a 62-mile round trip from his home in Ynysddu. "I'd love to have a hybrid car but even an entry-level used car is too expensive."The 48-year-old, who is married with a 12-year-old daughter, says he has to find the extra money for fuel "from an already tight budget" and "dreads" filling up at the pump."The best thing they could do at the Budget is drastically remove or reduce fuel duty for a period of time."The main fuel duty rate has been frozen at 57.95p per litre since March 2011, but Dave says: "It sounds like they're giving us something by keeping it frozen but they're actually still taking it off us."'I earn £150,000 and would be happy to pay more tax'Jonathan Whitwam, who recently joined the Labour Party, works in finance and says, in addition to his mortgage, his biggest outgoing is supporting his two daughters through university. He and his wife, who live in Essex, pay their rent, which is around £18,000 per year.His daughters will start their working lives with between £45,000 to £60,000 of debt each, plus interest, which will be compounding at £5,000 to £8,000 per year."I have no objection to paying for degrees as I think they are a great way of broadening horizons and having great life experience. But I think the interest should be waived or capped below 1%, otherwise it's a noose around their neck for a substantial part of their lifetime."More generally, Jonathan, 52, would welcome taxes being put up for higher earners like himself in the name of "redistribution". He would also like to see a one-off wealth tax for people with assets worth over £10m and new taxes on the oil and gas and banking sectors."If we want better roads, hospitals, schools we need to raise more tax."'I have a £15,000 pension. I'm spending more of my savings'Christine Morris, from Worksop, has been retired for eight years and lives on a state pension combined with a small private pension her late husband left her. "It is very difficult to balance the books," the 78-year-old says. "I do go on holiday, but I'm spending more of my savings to live."Although the prime minister has asked ministers to look at removing standing charges from gas bills, Christine thinks there should be some relief for people who live alone when it comes to standing charges on electricity bills, which are typically higher.She would also like the government to extend access to pension credit, external, a means-tested benefit for people who have reached state pension age and are receiving £238 or less per week. Christine currently receives £241 and so just misses out.She was unconvinced by Andy Burnham's pledge to end the triple lock so that from 2030 the state pension will rise at least by inflation or 2.5%, with the money saved used to create a free-at-the-point of use national care service for England sometime "in the next parliament".Christine thinks the new service will take time to come in. In the meantime, she fears she will "get less pension and still have to pay out the same for any care I need".Get in touchWhat are you hoping for from the Budget? What questions do you have?
